newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton to arrive in Australia for talks, and golf.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to arrive in Australia for talks, and golf.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton arrives in Australia on Tuesday at the start of his first overseas trip since his re-election, but his visit will see golf and watersports taking up more time than bilateral talks.
In fact, the local media have dubbed the state visit the "talking and snorkelling" trip.

Clinton, accompanied by his wife Hillary, is due to arrive in Sydney at 7.15 p.m (0815 GMT) and will spend four days visiting Sydney, Canberra and the Great Barrier Reef, before attending the APEC summit in the Philippines.
But Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Tuesday he he would raise serious trade issues with Clinton in a one-hour meeting on Wednesday in the national capital Canberra.
Howard said it was unfair that primary industries in the United States, Japan and Europe were subsidised by governments.

"I will be of course talking to the president about the continued discrimination against agriculture exports in world trading arrangements," Howard said. Australia, like the United States, is a major agricultural exporter.

In 1992, thousands of Australian wheat farmers staged noisy demonstrations against visiting former U.S. president George Bush to protest against a U.S. trade programme -- the Export Enhancement Programme -- which subsidises U.S. grain sales.

"The inefficient producers of primary produce get help from their governments, such as the Europeans and on occasions the Americans and Japanese...and that subsidised produce is then really dumped into our markets (and) we lose them," Howard said.

"If we were to turn around and do the same thing with some of our manufacturing exports we would be in trouble under world trade rules and that is the unfair and unbalanced world trading scene," Howard said. "And that kind of thing I will certainly talk about (with Clinton)."

Australia's trade balance is nearly four to one in favour of the United States. Australian merchandise exports to the United States were valued at A$4.6 billion (US$3.6 billion) in 1995, while U.S. imports into Australia stood at A$16.7 billion.
Clinton is the third American president to visit Australia after Lyndon Johnson and George Bush.
After meeting Howard, Clinton will address a joint sitting of both houses of the parliament, where he will reaffirm the long-standing alliance between the United States and Australia.
Clinton is also expected to thank Australia for its help in achieving the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty earlier this year and its cooperation on World Trade Organisation issues.
But for Clinton, trade talk is likely to be left to APEC in Subic Bay in the Philippines next week where forum leaders will discuss the group's pact to axe trade barriers by 2020.
For Clinton the prospect of a round of golf with the world's number one Greg Norman is a major attraction on the visit.
The president's itinerary has him free on Thursday afternoon, while Hillary speaks at the Sydney Opera House, and Norman is in town for the Australian Open golf tournament.

After a round of golf and a Sydney Harbour cruise, the Clintons will be to Port Douglas on the far northeast coast for the Clintons and two days of sun, snorkelling -- and probably Both Howard and Clinton will have China -- the allies both have strained relations with Beijing -- on their minds during the current visit. Both leaders will meet China's President Jiang Zemin at the APEC summit.
China has accused the United States of using Australia and Japan in an unofficial policy of containment, citing stronger defence ties between Canberra and Washington.

"We value the fact that China invests more in Australia than any other country," Howard said in The Sydney Morning Herald on Tuesday. "We want a good relationship...I certainly don't want to see China isolated," he said.
